vsm2.12:26.1:
(iv) A distinction brought about by the influence of knowledge either before the arising of the knowledge or after
it or at that moment is called success by intervention of knowledge;
vsm2.12:26.2:
for this is said: “The meaning (purpose) as abandoning perception of permanence succeeds through
contemplation of impermanence, thus it is success by intervention of knowledge … The meaning (purpose) as abandoning
all defilements succeeds through the Arahant path, thus it is success by intervention of knowledge.
vsm2.12:26.3: There was success by intervention of knowledge in the venerable Bakkula.
vsm2.12:26.4: There was success by intervention of knowledge in the venerable Saṅkicca.
vsm2.12:26.5: There was success by intervention of knowledge in the venerable Bhūtapāla” (Paṭis II 211).
vsm2.12:27.1:
Herein, when the venerable Bakkula as an infant was being bathed in the river on an auspicious day,
he fell into the stream through the negligence of his nurse.
vsm2.12:27.2: A fish swallowed him and eventually came to the bathing place at Benares.
vsm2.12:27.3: There it was caught by a fisherman and sold to a rich man’s wife.
vsm2.12:27.4:
The fish interested her, and thinking to cook it herself, she slit it open. When she did so, she saw the child
like a golden image in the fish’s stomach. She was overjoyed, thinking, “At last I have got a son.”
vsm2.12:27.5:
So the venerable Bakkula’s safe survival in a fish’s stomach in his last existence is called “success by intervention of knowledge”
because it was brought about by the influence of the Arahant-path knowledge due to be obtained by him in that life.
vsm2.12:27.6: But the story should be told in detail (see M-a IV 190).
vsm2.12:28.1: The Elder Saṅkicca’s mother died while he was still in her womb.
vsm2.12:28.2:
At the time of her cremation she was pierced by stakes and placed on a pyre. The infant received
a wound on the corner of his eye from the point of a stake and made a sound.
vsm2.12:28.3: Then, thinking that the child must be alive, they took down the body and opened its belly. They gave the child to the grandmother.
vsm2.12:28.4: Under her care he grew up, and eventually he went forth and reached Arahantship together with the discriminations.
vsm2.12:28.5:
So the venerable Saṅkicca’s safe survival on the pyre is called,
“success by intervention of knowledge” in the way just stated (see Dhp-a II 240).
vsm2.12:29.1: The boy Bhūtapāla’s father was a poor man in Rājagaha.
vsm2.12:29.2: He went into the forest with a cart to get a load of wood. It was evening when he returned to the city gate.
vsm2.12:29.3: Then his oxen slipped the yoke and escaped into the city.
vsm2.12:29.4: He seated the child beside the cart and went into the city after the oxen.
vsm2.12:29.5: Before he could come out again, the gate was closed.
vsm2.12:29.6:
The child’s safe survival through the three watches of the night outside the city in a place infested by wild
beasts and spirits is called, “success by intervention of knowledge” in the way just stated.
vsm2.12:29.7: But the story should be told in detail.
vsm2.12:30.1:
(v) A distinction brought about by the influence of serenity either before the concentration or after
it or at that moment is called success by intervention of concentration for this is said:
vsm2.12:30.2:
“The meaning (purpose) as abandoning the hindrances succeeds by means of the first jhāna, thus it is success by intervention
of concentration … The meaning (purpose) as abandoning the base consisting of nothingness succeeds by means of the attainment
of the base consisting of neither perception nor non-perception, thus it is success by intervention of concentration.
vsm2.12:30.3:
There was success by intervention of concentration in the venerable Sāriputta … in the venerable Sañjīva … in the venerable
Khāṇu-Kondañña … in the laywoman devotee Uttarā … in the lay-woman devotee Sāmāvatī” (Paṭis II 211–12).
vsm2.12:31.1:
Herein, while the venerable Sāriputta was living with the Elder Mahā Moggallāna at Kapotakandarā
he was sitting in the open on a moonlit night with his hair newly cut. Then a wicked spirit, though
warned by his companion, gave him a blow on the head, the noise of which was like a thunder clap.
vsm2.12:31.2: At the time the blow was given the elder was absorbed in an attainment;
vsm2.12:31.3: consequently he suffered no harm from the blow.
vsm2.12:31.4: This was success by intervention of concentration in that venerable one.
vsm2.12:31.5: The story is given in the Udāna too (Ud 39).
vsm2.12:32.1:
While the Elder Sañjīva was in the attainment of cessation, cowherds, etc., who noticed him thought
he was dead. They brought grass and sticks and cow-dung and set fire to them.
vsm2.12:32.2: Not even a corner of the elder’s robe was burnt.
vsm2.12:32.3:
This was success by intervention of concentration in him because it was brought about by the influence of the serenity
occurring in his successive attainment of each of the eight jhānas preceding cessation.
vsm2.12:32.4: But the story is given in the Suttas too (M I 333).
vsm2.12:33.1: The Elder Khāṇu Kondañña was naturally gifted in attainments.
vsm2.12:33.2: He was sitting absorbed in attainment one night in a certain forest.
vsm2.12:33.3:
Five hundred robbers came by with stolen booty. Thinking that no one was following them and needing rest,
they put the booty down. Believing the elder was a tree stump (khāṇuka), they piled all the booty on him.
vsm2.12:33.4:
The elder emerged at the predetermined time just as they were about to depart after resting, at the very
time in fact when the one who had put his booty down first was picking it up.
vsm2.12:33.5: When they saw the elder move, they cried out in fear.
vsm2.12:33.6: The elder said, “Do not be afraid, lay followers; I am a bhikkhu.”
vsm2.12:33.7:
They came and paid homage. Such was their confidence in the elder that they went forth into homelessness, and they
eventually reached Arahantship together with the discriminations.
vsm2.12:33.8:
The absence here of harm to the elder, covered as he was by five hundred bundles of goods,
was success by intervention of concentration (see Dhp-a II 254).
vsm2.12:34.1: The laywoman devotee Uttarā was the daughter of a rich man called Puṇṇaka.
vsm2.12:34.2: A harlot called Sirimā who was envious of her, poured a basin of hot oil over her head.
vsm2.12:34.3: At that moment Uttarā had attained jhāna in, loving-kindness.
vsm2.12:34.4: The oil ran off her like water on a lotus leaf.
vsm2.12:34.5: This was success by intervention of concentration in her.
vsm2.12:34.6: But the story should be given in detail (see Dhp-a III 310; A-a I 451).
vsm2.12:35.1: King Udena’s chief queen was called Sāmāvatī.
vsm2.12:35.2:
The brahman Māgaṇḍiya, who aspired to elevate his own daughter to the position of chief queen, put a poisonous snake into Sāmāvatī’s
lute. Then he told the king, “Sāmāvatī wants to kill you, sire. She is carrying a poisonous snake about in her lute.”
vsm2.12:35.3: When the king found it, he was furious. Intending to kill her, he took his bow and aimed a poisoned arrow.
vsm2.12:35.4: Sāmāvatī with her retinue pervaded the king with loving-kindness.
vsm2.12:35.5: The king stood trembling, unable either to shoot the arrow or to put it away.
vsm2.12:35.6: Then the queen said to him, “What is it, sire, are you tired?”—“Yes, I am tired.”—“Then put down the bow.”
vsm2.12:35.7: The arrow fell at the king’s feet.
vsm2.12:35.8: Then the queen advised him, “Sire, one should not hate one who has no hate.”
vsm2.12:35.9:
So the king’s not daring to release the arrow was success by intervention of concentration in the laywoman
Sāmāvatī (see Dhp-a I 216; A-a I 443).
vsm2.12:36.1: (vi) That which consists in dwelling perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive, etc., is called Noble Ones’ success,
vsm2.12:36.2:
according as it is said: “What is Noble Ones’ success? Here, if a bhikkhu should wish,
“May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive,” he dwells perceiving the unrepulsive in that …
he dwells in equanimity towards that, mindful and fully aware” (Paṭis II 212).
vsm2.12:36.3: This is called “Noble Ones’ success” because it is only produced in Noble Ones who have reached mind mastery.
vsm2.12:37.1:
For if a bhikkhu with cankers destroyed possesses this kind of success, then when in the case of a disagreeable object he
is practicing pervasion with loving-kindness or giving attention to it as elements, he dwells perceiving the unrepulsive;
vsm2.12:37.2:
or when in the case of an agreeable object he is practicing pervasion with foulness or giving
attention to it as impermanent, he dwells perceiving the repulsive.
vsm2.12:37.3:
Likewise, when in the case of the repulsive and unrepulsive he is practicing that same
pervasion with loving-kindness or giving attention to it as elements, he dwells perceiving the unrepulsive;
vsm2.12:37.4:
and when in the case of the unrepulsive and repulsive he is practicing that same pervasion with foulness or giving
attention to it as impermanent, he dwells perceiving the repulsive. But when he is exercising the six-factored
equanimity in the following way, “On seeing a visible object with the eye, he is neither glad nor …” (Paṭis II 213),
etc., then rejecting both the repulsive and the unrepulsive, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and fully aware.
vsm2.12:38.1:
For the meaning of this is expounded in the Paṭisambhidā in the way beginning: “How does he dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the
repulsive? In the case of a disagreeable object he pervades it with loving-kindness or he treats it as elements” (Paṭis II 212).
vsm2.12:38.2: Thus it is called, “Noble Ones’ success” because it is only produced in Noble Ones who have reached mind mastery.
vsm2.12:39.1: (vii) That consisting in travelling through the air in the case of winged birds, etc., is called success born of kamma result,
vsm2.12:39.2:
according as it is said: “What is success born of kamma result? That in all winged birds, in all deities, in some
human beings, in some inhabitants of states of loss, is success born of kamma result” (Paṭis II 213).
vsm2.12:39.3:
For here it is the capacity in all winged birds to travel through the air without
jhāna or insight that is success born of kamma result;
vsm2.12:39.4: and likewise that in all deities, and some human beings, at the beginning of the aeon,
vsm2.12:39.5:
and likewise that in some inhabitants of states of loss such as the female spirit Piyaṅkara’s mother
(see S-a II 509), Uttara’s mother (Pv 140), Phussamittā, Dhammaguttā, and so on.
vsm2.12:40.1:
(viii) That consisting in travelling through the air, etc., in the case of Wheel-turning
Monarchs, etc., is called success of the meritorious,
vsm2.12:40.2:
according as it is said: “What is success of the meritorious? The Wheel-turning Monarch travels
through the air with his fourfold army, even with his grooms and shepherds.
vsm2.12:40.3: The householder Jotika had the success of the meritorious.
vsm2.12:40.4: The householder Jaṭilaka had the success of the meritorious.
vsm2.12:40.5: The householder Ghosita had the success of the meritorious.
vsm2.12:40.6: The householder Meṇḍaka had the success of the meritorious.
vsm2.12:40.7: That of the five very meritorious is success of the meritorious” (Paṭis II 213).
vsm2.12:40.8:
In brief, however, it is the distinction that consists in succeeding when the accumulated
merit comes to ripen that is success of the meritorious.
vsm2.12:41.1:
A crystal palace and sixty-four wishing trees cleft the earth and sprang into existence for the householder Jotika.
That was success of the meritorious in his case (Dhp-a IV 207).
vsm2.12:41.2: A golden rock of eighty cubits high was made for Jaṭilaka (Dhp-a IV 216).
vsm2.12:41.3: Ghosita’s safe survival when attempts were made in seven places to kill him was success of the meritorious (Dhp-a I 174).
vsm2.12:41.4:
The appearance to Meṇḍaka (= Ram) of rams (meṇḍaka) made of the seven gems in a place
the size of one sītā was success of the meritorious in Meṇḍaka (Dhp-a III 364).
vsm2.12:42.1:
The “five very meritorious” are the rich man Meṇḍaka, his wife Candapadumasiri, his son the rich
man Dhanañjaya, his daughter-in-law Sumanadevī, and his slave Puṇṇa.
vsm2.12:42.2:
When the rich man Meṇḍaka washed his head and looked up at the sky, twelve thousand five
hundred measures were filled for him with red rice from the sky.
vsm2.12:42.3: When his wife took a nāḷi measure of cooked rice, the food was not used up though she served the whole of Jambudīpa with it.
vsm2.12:42.4:
When his son took a purse containing a thousand ducats (kahāpaṇa), the ducats were not exhausted
even though he made gifts to all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa.
vsm2.12:42.5:
When his daughter-in-law took a pint (tumba) measure of paddy, the grain was not used up
even when she shared it out among all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa.
vsm2.12:42.6: When the slave ploughed with a single ploughshare, there were fourteen furrows, seven on each side (see Vin I 240; Dhp-a I 384).
vsm2.12:42.7: This was success of the meritorious in them.
vsm2.12:43.1: (ix) That beginning with travelling through the air in the case of masters of the sciences is success through the sciences,
vsm2.12:43.2:
according as it is said: “What is success through the sciences? Masters of the sciences, having pronounced their scientific spells,
travel through the air, and they show an elephant in space, in the sky … and they show a manifold military array” (Paṭis II 213).
vsm2.12:44.1:
(x) But the succeeding of such and such work through such and such right exertion
is success in the sense of succeeding due to right exertion applied here or there,
vsm2.12:44.2:
according as it is said: “The meaning (purpose) of abandoning lust succeeds through renunciation, thus it is success in the sense
of succeeding due to right exertion applied here or there … The meaning (purpose) of abandoning all defilements succeeds through
the Arahant path, thus it is success in the sense of succeeding due to right exertion applied here or there” (Paṭis II 213).
vsm2.12:44.3: And the text here is similar to the previous text in the illustration of right exertion, in other words, the way.
vsm2.12:44.4:
But in the Commentary it is given as follows: “Any work belonging to a trade such as making a cart assemblage, etc., any medical
work, the learning of the Three Vedas, the learning of the Three Piṭakas, even any work connected with ploughing, sowing,
etc.—the distinction produced by doing such work is success in the sense of succeeding due to right exertion applied here or there.”
vsm2.12:45.1:
So, among these ten kinds of success, only (i) success by resolve is actually
mentioned in the clause “kinds of supernormal power (success),”
vsm2.12:45.2: but (ii) success as transformation and (iii) success as the mind-made body are needed in this sense as well.
vsm2.12:46.1: (i) To the kinds of supernormal power (see §20): to the components of supernormal power, or to the departments of supernormal power.
vsm2.12:46.2:
He directs, he inclines, his mind: when that bhikkhu’s consciousness has become the basis for direct-knowledge in the way
already described, he directs the preliminary-work consciousness with the purpose of attaining the kinds of supernormal power,
he sends it in the direction of the kinds of supernormal power, leading it away from the kasiṇa as its object.
vsm2.12:46.3: Inclines: makes it tend and lean towards the supernormal power to be attained.
vsm2.12:47.1: He: the bhikkhu who has done the directing of his mind in this way.
vsm2.12:47.2: The various: varied, of different sorts.
vsm2.12:47.3: Kinds of supernormal power: departments of supernormal power.
vsm2.12:47.4: Wields: paccanubhoti = paccanu-bhavati (alternative form); the meaning is that he makes contact with, realizes, reaches.
vsm2.12:48.1:
Now, in order to show that variousness, it is said: “Having been one, he becomes many; having been many,
he becomes one. He appears and vanishes. He goes unhindered through walls, through enclosures, through mountains,
as though in open space. He dives in and out of the earth as though in water. He goes on unbroken water as though on earth.
Seated cross-legged he travels in space like a winged bird. With his hand he touches and strokes the moon and sun
so mighty and powerful. He wields bodily mastery even as far as the Brahmā-world” (D I 77).
vsm2.12:48.2: Herein, having been one: having been normally one before giving effect to the supernormal power.
vsm2.12:48.3:
He becomes many: wanting to walk with many or wanting to do a recital or wanting to ask
questions with many, he becomes a hundred or a thousand.
vsm2.12:48.4: But how does he do this?
vsm2.12:48.5:
He accomplishes, (1) the four planes, (2) the four bases (roads), (3) the eight steps, and (4)
the sixteen roots of supernormal power, and then he (5) resolves with knowledge.
